## Purpose and outcomes

Use Linux/POSIX interfaces as resource/lifetime protocols. Own descriptors and mappings, handle partial operations and separate visible state from durability and implementation-specific behavior. The intended result is a mechanism you can explain, a bounded artifact you can inspect and an evidence trail someone else can reproduce.

## Entry check and remediation

Track two handles sharing one abstract offset and explain a short byte transfer. Revisit T18 ownership/error contracts and T07 environment setup if either result is treated as a simple all-or-nothing call. Use [guide-entry](#guide-entry) for diagnostic evidence and [guide-roadmap](#guide-roadmap) for route choices. Domain numbers are coverage IDs, not an instruction to study them numerically.

## Component progression

**A process and descriptor ownership ledger.** Trace creation, inheritance, sharing, close, mapping and synchronization at actual system-call boundaries. Keep returned bytes, file offsets and persistence claims distinct.

Before implementation, predict this discriminating case: **An inherited write descriptor keeping a pipe alive after the apparent producer exits.** Carry its evidence into the projects below. Reuse one accepted component revision; new projects charge their new mechanism or experiment, not a second implementation of the old one.

Follow the [project route](#guide-project-route) for ordering. Domain numbers are reference categories. The [laboratory](#guide-laboratory) and [shared contract cards](#guide-component-contracts) separate automatic execution from reasoning, transfer and physical observations.

## Study sequence and teaching

Work through the mechanism notes in order within each project, alternating hand prediction with observation. Preserve the first counterexample rather than only a final green test. Full implementations belong to the projects; these notes explain what they must establish.


<a id="t23-01"></a>

### T23.01 — Process model

A process combines identity, an address space and credentials; threads share some of that state while keeping their own execution state. Arguments, environment and limits are inputs, not universal constants.

Investigate: Capture a child process context and label which facts are POSIX contracts and which are Linux observations. A common mistake is: A process and a thread are interchangeable isolation units. Evidence: A context manifest explains working directory, environment, limits and declared interfaces. Develop that evidence in [PR-T23-01](#pr-t23-01).

Retain a separate evidence item for each objective below. Meeting one objective does not establish the others.

### T23.02 — Process lifecycle

fork duplicates an execution context while exec replaces its program image. A failed exec returns in the child and must report failure without accidentally continuing the parent workflow. Threaded fork adds restricted child-side obligations.

Investigate: Implement a spawn/wait utility with a dedicated child-error channel and explicit inherited descriptors. A common mistake is: Successful fork implies successful execution of the requested program. Evidence: Exit and error records distinguish launch failure, child result and wait failure. Develop that evidence in [PR-T23-01](#pr-t23-01).

### T23.03 — Descriptors and open-file descriptions

A descriptor is one table entry; an open-file description contains shared offset/status state. Duplication can share that state while ownership of the descriptor numbers remains separate.

Investigate: Trace dup and fork inheritance, set close-on-exec deliberately and audit closure paths. A common mistake is: Duplicated descriptors have independent file offsets. Evidence: The synthetic ledger and observed positioned/sequential reads distinguish shared offset from handle lifetime. Develop that evidence in [PR-T23-01](#pr-t23-01).

<a id="t23-04"></a>

### T23.04 — Robust byte I/O

I/O adapters maintain progress and choose retry policy for the specific operation. EOF differs from would-block; a failed operation is not automatically safe to repeat unchanged.

Investigate: Implement robust byte-copy using scripted short transfers, interruptions and terminal failures. A common mistake is: read or write either handles the whole buffer or transfers nothing. Evidence: The output byte sequence and progress ledger contain neither omissions nor duplicate writes. Develop that evidence in [PR-T23-02](#pr-t23-02).

<a id="t23-05"></a>

### T23.05 — Paths and filesystem objects

A pathname is a lookup request through directory entries, not an object identity. An open handle can survive a rename/unlink, and a check-then-open sequence can race with namespace changes.

Investigate: Use a directory-relative operation and compare a renamed open file with a fresh path lookup. A common mistake is: Checking a path once authorizes all later uses of that name. Evidence: An identity/lookup trace states symlink policy and avoids unsupported race-free claims. Develop that evidence in [PR-T23-02](#pr-t23-02).

Creation permissions combine requested mode with a mask and the actual authorization environment. A successful lookup says nothing by itself about permission for the next operation.

Evidence: Expected bit arithmetic and actual metadata are separated from ownership/ACL/environment effects. Develop that evidence in [PR-T23-02](#pr-t23-02).

Sequential operations update shared offset state; positioned I/O supplies an explicit offset without using that cursor. Sparse holes affect logical size without storing every byte physically.

A virtual mapping reserves address ranges and protection, while residency depends on page faults and backing. Copy-on-write separates modifications after fork without requiring immediate eager copies.

Investigate: Compare untouched/touched anonymous pages and one protection change in a disposable child. A common mistake is: mmap success proves every page is physically resident. Evidence: The report labels virtual extent, fault observations and residency measurements by their limits. Develop that evidence in [PR-T23-03](#pr-t23-03).

### T23.09 — Memory-mapped files

A mapping borrows a bounded file extent whose backing can change. Truncation can make a formerly mapped access fault; cleanup owns both mapping length and descriptor policy.

Investigate: Implement a bounded mapped-reader contract and exercise truncation only inside a disposable child. A common mistake is: Mapping a file permanently freezes its size and contents. Evidence: Failure classification, mapping bounds and cleanup ownership are explicit before any access. Develop that evidence in [PR-T23-03](#pr-t23-03).

Shared bytes require shared representation and a synchronization contract. A process-local pointer cannot be interpreted at another mapping address; offsets plus checked bounds make layout relocatable.

### T23.11 — Pipes and terminal I/O

Pipeline ends must close unused descriptors or EOF can never arrive. Backpressure is ordinary flow control; terminal modes add line processing that should be restored after use.

Investigate: Build a two-stage pipeline and a pseudoterminal experiment with an explicit restoration path. A common mistake is: An idle reader always gets EOF when the visible writer exits. Evidence: Descriptor closure diagrams explain blocking, broken-pipe behavior and terminal-state restoration. Develop that evidence in [PR-T23-04](#pr-t23-04).

<a id="t23-12"></a>

### T23.12 — Persistence and crash consistency

Buffered success, interprocess visibility and durable storage are distinct claims. A replacement protocol needs an ordered sequence and filesystem-specific durability assumptions.

Worked update boundary: after writing and synchronizing a temporary file, renaming it changes the visible namespace. Synchronizing the containing directory is a separate step for the directory entry. Termination between those operations creates different evidence obligations; a test that observes the new content after ordinary process termination is not a power-loss experiment. A stable separate lockfile avoids changing the locked inode during replacement.

Investigate: Specify a temporary-file/write/synchronize/rename protocol and inject interruption at each declared step. A common mistake is: A successful write or rename universally proves durable data. Evidence: A crash-state matrix states old/new/partial possibilities and names unverified filesystem guarantees. Develop that evidence in [PR-T23-05](#pr-t23-05).

The essential spine below is deliberately narrow. Assign only the exact inspected registry locators shown; no whole book, standard or implementation is implied. Historical rationale does not replace a current contract, and one implementation does not create a portable guarantee. - **The Linux Programming Interface: A Linux and UNIX System Programming Handbook (First edition)** — `R-SYS-TLPI-2010`, exactly **§3.4 Handling Errors from System Calls and Library Functions, pp. 48–55** (1 h). Separate syscall failure, progress and wrapper error conventions. Compare the source claim with your project assumptions. The registry classifies this as primary; its inspection limits remain part of the assignment.

The registry classifies this as primary; its inspection limits remain part of the assignment.

- **Linux man-pages: selected user-space interface contracts (Linux man-pages 6.19; HTML captured 4 October 2026)** — `R-SYS-LINUX-MAN-6-19`, exactly **read(2) — DESCRIPTION, RETURN VALUE, ERRORS** (1 h). <a id="t24"></a>

# T24 — Signals, IPC, networking, and event-driven systems

| Track | Status | Hours | Dependency profiles |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| linux | core | 77 | A, C |

**Prerequisites:** [T23](#t23), [T15](#t15).

| Reading | Implementation | Verification | Assessment | Consolidation |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 3 | 46 | 20 | 4 | 4 |

## Purpose and outcomes

Turn asynchronous notifications into bounded state machines with clear buffer/descriptor ownership. Local-only transport labs separate stream framing, datagrams, readiness, signal safety and shutdown. The intended result is a mechanism you can explain, a bounded artifact you can inspect and an evidence trail someone else can reproduce. The published workload includes 6 h of explicitly elective project work; a core-only route subtracts those project hours, without removing core awareness.

## Entry check and remediation

Pass robust byte I/O and the T15 incremental-parser chunk-split cases first. If one read is still treated as one message, redo those cases before opening sockets. Use [guide-entry](#guide-entry) for diagnostic evidence and [guide-roadmap](#guide-roadmap) for route choices. Domain numbers are coverage IDs, not an instruction to study them numerically.

## Component progression

**An event loop with generation identities.** Define readiness, bounded work, deadlines and continuation state. Reconstruct partial I/O and stale notifications with a deterministic adapter before using live descriptors.

Before implementation, predict this discriminating case: **An event for an old descriptor number arriving after that number has been reused.** Carry its evidence into the projects below. Reuse one accepted component revision; new projects charge their new mechanism or experiment, not a second implementation of the old one.

Follow the [project route](#guide-project-route) for ordering. Domain numbers are reference categories. The [laboratory](#guide-laboratory) and [shared contract cards](#guide-component-contracts) separate automatic execution from reasoning, transfer and physical observations.

## Study sequence and teaching

Work through the mechanism notes in order within each project, alternating hand prediction with observation. Preserve the first counterexample rather than only a final green test. Full implementations belong to the projects; these notes explain what they must establish.


<a id="t24-01"></a>

### T24.01 — Signal model

Signals have generation, pending and delivery stages; a mask delays delivery and a disposition chooses its action. Restart policy does not make arbitrary interrupted operations safely repeatable.

Investigate: Install a minimal handler with an explicitly allowed action and compare masking with pending delivery. A common mistake is: Signal handlers can use ordinary stdio because only one handler runs at a time. Evidence: A timeline and safety allowlist explain every handler operation and retry decision. Develop that evidence in [PR-T24-01](#pr-t24-01).


#### Evidence checklist

Retain a separate evidence item for each objective below. Meeting one objective does not establish the others.


<a id="t24-01-a"></a>


- **T24.01.a** Distinguish generation, pending state, masking, and delivery. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T24-01](#pr-t24-01).


<a id="t24-01-b"></a>


- **T24.01.b** Install handlers with explicit disposition and restart policies. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T24-01](#pr-t24-01).


<a id="t24-01-c"></a>


- **T24.01.c** Limit handler operations to the applicable safety contract. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T24-01](#pr-t24-01).


<a id="t24-02"></a>

### T24.02 — Race-free signal integration

Checking a shutdown flag and then sleeping can lose a notification between the two actions. Atomic mask-and-wait, a self-pipe or a synchronous signal interface closes that gap under different contracts.

Investigate: Construct the lost-wakeup schedule, then implement one design with coordinated thread masks. A common mistake is: Adding a volatile flag closes the sleep race. Evidence: A deterministic schedule demonstrates the broken window and the repaired wakeup/ownership path. Develop that evidence in [PR-T24-01](#pr-t24-01).


#### Evidence checklist

Retain a separate evidence item for each objective below. Meeting one objective does not establish the others.


<a id="t24-02-a"></a>


- **T24.02.a** Compare atomic waiting, self-pipe, and signalfd designs. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T24-01](#pr-t24-01).


<a id="t24-02-b"></a>


- **T24.02.b** Coordinate signal masks across threads. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T24-01](#pr-t24-01).


<a id="t24-02-c"></a>


- **T24.02.c** Eliminate lost-wakeup windows during shutdown and child handling. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T24-01](#pr-t24-01).


<a id="t24-03"></a>

### T24.03 — IPC selection

IPC choice specifies isolation, message boundaries, storage ownership and failure discovery. Shared memory avoids some copies but moves synchronization and participant recovery into the application.

Investigate: Compare a bounded pipe, local socket and shared-record design for one request/reply workload. A common mistake is: The fastest nominal transport is always the simplest reliable choice. Evidence: A selection matrix includes stalled-peer backpressure and ownership after disconnect. Develop that evidence in [PR-T24-02](#pr-t24-02).


#### Evidence checklist

Retain a separate evidence item for each objective below. Meeting one objective does not establish the others.


<a id="t24-03-a"></a>


- **T24.03.a** Compare pipes, local sockets, shared memory, and queues. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T24-02](#pr-t24-02).


<a id="t24-03-b"></a>


- **T24.03.b** Define message boundaries, ownership, and failure notification. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T24-02](#pr-t24-02).


<a id="t24-03-c"></a>


- **T24.03.c** Select mechanisms against latency, isolation, and backpressure needs. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T24-02](#pr-t24-02).


<a id="t24-04"></a>

### T24.04 — Socket lifecycle

Socket creation and connection are state transitions that each acquire or release a descriptor. Address resolution can produce several candidates, and IPv4/IPv6/local names need different representations.

Investigate: Implement a loopback/local-only client/server setup that cleans up every failed candidate. A common mistake is: connect success or accept failure leaves all descriptor ownership obvious. Evidence: A descriptor ledger and failure injection show exactly one owner for each live handle. Develop that evidence in [PR-T24-02](#pr-t24-02).


#### Evidence checklist

Retain a separate evidence item for each objective below. Meeting one objective does not establish the others.


<a id="t24-04-a"></a>


- **T24.04.a** Manage address resolution, creation, bind, listen, accept, and connect. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T24-02](#pr-t24-02).


<a id="t24-04-b"></a>


- **T24.04.b** Track every descriptor through failure and shutdown paths. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T24-02](#pr-t24-02).


<a id="t24-04-c"></a>


- **T24.04.c** Compare IPv4, IPv6, and local-domain addressing assumptions. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T24-02](#pr-t24-02).


<a id="t24-05"></a>

### T24.05 — TCP stream protocols

TCP transports ordered bytes rather than application records. Frames may be split or combined; half-close stops one direction while queued work and the other direction can remain live.

Investigate: Run a length-framed protocol over arbitrary byte chunks with a bounded output queue and explicit reconnect policy. A common mistake is: One send corresponds to one receive. Evidence: All chunk splits preserve frames; half-close and stalled peers follow the stated queue bounds. Develop that evidence in [PR-T24-03](#pr-t24-03).


#### Evidence checklist

Retain a separate evidence item for each objective below. Meeting one objective does not establish the others.


<a id="t24-05-a"></a>


- **T24.05.a** Separate byte-stream transport from application messages. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T24-03](#pr-t24-03).


<a id="t24-05-b"></a>


- **T24.05.b** Implement framing, partial transfer, half-close, and reconnect policy. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T24-03](#pr-t24-03).


<a id="t24-05-c"></a>


- **T24.05.c** Bound queued data and stalled-peer resource use. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T24-03](#pr-t24-03).


<a id="t24-06"></a>

### T24.06 — UDP and datagrams

UDP preserves datagram boundaries but delivery, duplication and order belong to a higher-level policy. Truncated reception must not be mistaken for a valid complete message.

Investigate: Implement a tiny sequence-numbered datagram exercise with declared drop/duplicate handling. A common mistake is: Local send success acknowledges remote processing. Evidence: A scripted loss/reorder trace produces the declared acceptance set and visible truncation errors. Develop that evidence in [PR-T24-03](#pr-t24-03).


#### Evidence checklist

Retain a separate evidence item for each objective below. Meeting one objective does not establish the others.


<a id="t24-06-a"></a>


- **T24.06.a** Preserve message boundaries and handle truncation explicitly. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T24-03](#pr-t24-03).


<a id="t24-06-b"></a>


- **T24.06.b** Design sequencing, duplicate handling, and loss policies where required. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T24-03](#pr-t24-03).


<a id="t24-06-c"></a>


- **T24.06.c** Separate local send success from remote delivery evidence. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T24-03](#pr-t24-03).


<a id="t24-07"></a>

### T24.07 — Nonblocking execution

Nonblocking state machines retain cursors and ownership between readiness notifications. Would-block is a state transition, not a busy-wait invitation or an error that resets progress.

Investigate: Implement partial receive/transmit cursors and a per-turn work quota. A common mistake is: Readiness guarantees the entire pending operation completes. Evidence: The scripted backend verifies bounded turns, exact byte progress and eventual handling of another ready connection. Develop that evidence in [PR-T24-04](#pr-t24-04).


#### Evidence checklist

Retain a separate evidence item for each objective below. Meeting one objective does not establish the others.


<a id="t24-07-a"></a>


- **T24.07.a** Model readiness, would-block, partial progress, and completion. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T24-04](#pr-t24-04).


<a id="t24-07-b"></a>


- **T24.07.b** Maintain operation state across event-loop iterations. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T24-04](#pr-t24-04).


<a id="t24-07-c"></a>


- **T24.07.c** Prevent busy loops and unfair starvation of other connections. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T24-04](#pr-t24-04).


<a id="t24-08"></a>

### T24.08 — poll and epoll

Level triggering reports readiness while it persists; edge triggering requires consuming progress until would-block under its contract. Descriptor reuse can make stale events refer to a new logical connection.

Investigate: Implement an LT loop first, then analyze or add ET draining with generation-tagged connection state. A common mistake is: An event’s descriptor number permanently identifies one connection. Evidence: The event trace rejects a stale generation and explains every rearm/drain decision. Develop that evidence in [PR-T24-04](#pr-t24-04).


#### Evidence checklist

Retain a separate evidence item for each objective below. Meeting one objective does not establish the others.


<a id="t24-08-a"></a>


- **T24.08.a** Compare level-triggered and edge-triggered operation. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T24-04](#pr-t24-04).


<a id="t24-08-b"></a>


- **T24.08.b** Handle registration changes, descriptor reuse, and stale events. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T24-04](#pr-t24-04).


<a id="t24-08-c"></a>


- **T24.08.c** Design bounded work per event-loop turn. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T24-04](#pr-t24-04).


<a id="t24-09"></a>

### T24.09 — Timers and notifications

A timer expiry records a deadline event, while callback execution waits for scheduling. Counter-based notifications can accumulate more than one event between reads.

Investigate: Integrate a monotonic deadline queue and declared timer/event counter backend. A common mistake is: A callback ran exactly at the expiry timestamp. Evidence: Deadline, reported expiration count and actual dispatch time are recorded separately under cancellation/reschedule tests. Develop that evidence in [PR-T24-05](#pr-t24-05).


#### Evidence checklist

Retain a separate evidence item for each objective below. Meeting one objective does not establish the others.


<a id="t24-09-a"></a>


- **T24.09.a** Integrate timerfd, eventfd, and monotonic deadlines where appropriate. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T24-05](#pr-t24-05).


<a id="t24-09-b"></a>


- **T24.09.b** Distinguish timer expiry from actual handler execution time. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T24-05](#pr-t24-05).


<a id="t24-09-c"></a>


- **T24.09.c** Handle cancellation, rescheduling, and counter accumulation. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T24-05](#pr-t24-05).


<a id="t24-10"></a>

### T24.10 — Serial and embedded transports

Serial bytes share framing concerns with sockets but also require transport settings and timeout policy. SocketCAN experiments need a controlled virtual or bench bus, not assumptions about live equipment.

Investigate: Reuse the same parser through a pseudoterminal and test backend; analyze a declared virtual-CAN frame. A common mistake is: Changing the transport makes parser state and buffer limits irrelevant. Evidence: Identical parser vectors pass both backends, while baud/line/CAN assumptions remain separate from protocol logic. Develop that evidence in [PR-T24-06](#pr-t24-06).


#### Evidence checklist

Retain a separate evidence item for each objective below. Meeting one objective does not establish the others.


<a id="t24-10-a"></a>


- **T24.10.a** Configure a serial transport with explicit framing and timeout behavior. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T24-06](#pr-t24-06).


<a id="t24-10-b"></a>


- **T24.10.b** Reuse portable parsers between serial, network, and test backends. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T24-06](#pr-t24-06).


<a id="t24-10-c"></a>


- **T24.10.c** Explore SocketCAN using a controlled virtual or bench network. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T24-06](#pr-t24-06).


<a id="t24-11"></a>

### T24.11 — Graceful shutdown and overload

Shutdown is an ownership protocol: stop admission, decide whether queued work drains or cancels, notify blocked participants and release resources once. Overload needs a bounded policy before queues grow.

Investigate: Implement queue admission limits and repeated graceful-stop requests with a deadline. A common mistake is: Closing one listener automatically terminates every blocked operation. Evidence: A shutdown state trace accounts for every queued item, descriptor and cancellation result. Develop that evidence in [PR-T24-04](#pr-t24-04).


#### Evidence checklist

Retain a separate evidence item for each objective below. Meeting one objective does not establish the others.


<a id="t24-11-a"></a>


- **T24.11.a** Define admission limits, queue bounds, and load-shedding policy. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T24-04](#pr-t24-04).


<a id="t24-11-b"></a>


- **T24.11.b** Drain or cancel work with unambiguous ownership. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T24-04](#pr-t24-04).


<a id="t24-11-c"></a>


- **T24.11.c** Test blocked consumers, disappearing peers, and repeated shutdown requests. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T24-04](#pr-t24-04).


<a id="t24-12"></a>

### T24.12 — Advanced I/O

Advanced async I/O adds submission/completion and buffer lifetimes that differ from readiness loops. Copy avoidance may retain or pin buffers longer and does not erase ownership costs. This topic is elective; its implementation project is optional.

Investigate: Electively analyze a pinned io_uring version after inspecting its operation contract, or perform a bounded comparison with the existing event loop. A common mistake is: A newer API is faster for every workload. Evidence: The elective report names operation lifetime rules, complete-workload measurements and evidence limits; no uninspected operation is implemented. Develop that evidence in [PR-T24-07](#pr-t24-07).


#### Evidence checklist

Retain a separate evidence item for each objective below. Meeting one objective does not establish the others.


<a id="t24-12-a"></a>


- **T24.12.a** Investigate io_uring with version-specific operation and lifetime rules. **Disposition:** elective. **Activity:** [PR-T24-07](#pr-t24-07).


<a id="t24-12-b"></a>


- **T24.12.b** Compare copy avoidance with ownership and pinning costs. **Disposition:** elective. **Activity:** [PR-T24-07](#pr-t24-07).


<a id="t24-12-c"></a>


- **T24.12.c** Measure complete workloads before choosing a more complex interface. **Disposition:** elective. **Activity:** [PR-T24-07](#pr-t24-07).

## Purpose and outcomes

Design sharing and lifetimes before synchronization. Protect invariants, explain ordering edges and validate concrete schedules without treating a race detector or fast benchmark as proof. The intended result is a mechanism you can explain, a bounded artifact you can inspect and an evidence trail someone else can reproduce.

## Entry check and remediation

Draw the lifetime of a work item from creator to last consumer and identify a shared ordinary write/read pair. Review T18 ownership, T02 sequencing, T03 lifetime and T05 C11 atomic facilities before choosing memory orders. Use [guide-entry](#guide-entry) for diagnostic evidence and [guide-roadmap](#guide-roadmap) for route choices. Domain numbers are coverage IDs, not an instruction to study them numerically.

## Component progression

**A happens-before argument with a counterexample.** Write ownership and publication conditions before adding atomics. Draw conflicting accesses, predicate transitions and synchronization edges; test waiting and shutdown together.

Before implementation, predict this discriminating case: **A notification occurring before a waiter commits to sleep, or a relaxed flag publishing unfinished data.** Carry its evidence into the projects below. Reuse one accepted component revision; new projects charge their new mechanism or experiment, not a second implementation of the old one.

Follow the [project route](#guide-project-route) for ordering. Domain numbers are reference categories. The [laboratory](#guide-laboratory) and [shared contract cards](#guide-component-contracts) separate automatic execution from reasoning, transfer and physical observations.

## Study sequence and teaching

Work through the mechanism notes in order within each project, alternating hand prediction with observation. Preserve the first counterexample rather than only a final green test. Full implementations belong to the projects; these notes explain what they must establish.


<a id="t25-01"></a>

### T25.01 — Thread lifecycle

Creating a thread acquires execution and join/detach obligations. A joinable handle needs one join owner; detached execution instead needs an independent lifetime protocol for shared arguments. C and POSIX provide distinct start/result/status interfaces, whose handles and callbacks must not be interchanged.

Interface mapping for the selected C17 lesson: C thread facilities are optional; record __STDC_NO_THREADS__ and actual header/library support separately from POSIX availability. The inspected N3096 text is a later-draft cross-check, not an exact C17 edition. C uses thrd_t, thrd_create(thrd_t*, int (*)(void*), void*) and thrd_join(thrd_t, int*): the start returns an int, creation returns thrd_success/thrd_nomem/thrd_error and joining reports the integer result. POSIX uses pthread_t, pthread_create(pthread_t*, const pthread_attr_t*, void* (*)(void*), void*) and pthread_join(pthread_t, void**): null attributes request defaults, the start returns a pointer, and creation/join return zero or an error number directly. Keep the result pointee live independently; do not diagnose a nonzero pthread result by assuming errno contains it. Neither family supplies a portable representation cast to the other. Never mix their creation/start/join contracts, and do not join a detached or already-joined thread. PR-T25-01 implements one POSIX worker and supplies this comparison plus availability probes, rather than two worker implementations.

Investigate: Implement one POSIX worker lifecycle with explicit result storage; compare C/POSIX signatures, statuses and support through the bounded mapping below and compile-only availability probes. A common mistake is: A function argument remains live until any thread using it finishes, or C and POSIX thread APIs are interchangeable. Evidence: A lifetime table and failure paths show every shared argument/handle owner; the separate interface/support table preserves integer versus pointer results, optional C17 facility support and direct POSIX error statuses. Develop that evidence in [PR-T25-01](#pr-t25-01).

<a id="t25-02"></a>

### T25.02 — Shared-state design

Reducing shared mutable state makes ordering obligations smaller. Immutable inputs, per-thread results and explicitly transferred work items need different ownership transitions.

Investigate: Partition a workload and transfer caller-owned work items through a bounded queue. A common mistake is: Every object visible to several threads needs a fine-grained lock. Evidence: The shared-state ledger contains only deliberate shared fields and names the last user of each item. Develop that evidence in [PR-T25-01](#pr-t25-01).

<a id="t25-03"></a>

### T25.03 — Mutexes and invariants

A mutex protects an invariant spanning several fields. Locking each assignment separately can expose a state that satisfies neither the old nor the new invariant; lock ordering prevents a different class of failure.

Investigate: Protect a balance/queue-count invariant and establish a global lock order. A common mistake is: Atomic field updates automatically preserve a compound invariant. Evidence: A forced interleaving finds the broken split-lock version, and initialization/destruction waits for all users. Develop that evidence in [PR-T25-02](#pr-t25-02).

<a id="t25-04"></a>

### T25.04 — Condition variables

A condition variable is a notification mechanism, while a predicate under the mutex decides whether work may proceed. Wait releases and reacquires the mutex; successful return can still leave the predicate false.

Investigate: Implement a bounded producer/consumer queue with while-predicate waits, shutdown and an absolute timeout policy. A common mistake is: One signal transfers ownership of a guaranteed item. Evidence: Spurious wake and signal-before-wait schedules both preserve progress and shutdown ownership. Develop that evidence in [PR-T25-02](#pr-t25-02).

<a id="t25-05"></a>

### T25.05 — Other synchronization primitives

A semaphore counts available permits; a barrier coordinates a phase; a read/write lock separates access classes; once initialization establishes one publication boundary. Each needs its own fairness and failure assumptions.

Investigate: Compare them on fixed traces and implement one phase or permit example. A common mistake is: The API with the fewest calls necessarily matches the invariant. Evidence: A primitive-selection table states required semantics and avoids assuming fairness from mutual exclusion. Develop that evidence in [PR-T25-02](#pr-t25-02).

<a id="t25-06"></a>

### T25.06 — Data races and happens-before

Happens-before combines sequencing with the relevant synchronization relation. Race freedom orders conflicting ordinary accesses, but it does not establish an application invariant or a valid lifetime.

Investigate: Draw an execution graph and identify one missing edge, then repair publication. A common mistake is: No detected data race proves the algorithm is correct. Evidence: Graph reachability, lifetime annotations and a separate logical invariant support the conclusion. Develop that evidence in [PR-T25-03](#pr-t25-03).

<a id="t25-07"></a>

### T25.07 — Atomic objects and operations

Atomic operations make one object’s accesses participate in an atomic model. The implementation may use helper calls or locks for widths/alignment it cannot lower natively.

Investigate: Initialize/load/store/RMW an atomic counter and inspect its target-specific lock-free result and object dependencies. A common mistake is: Every atomic type is lock-free on every target. Evidence: A target report states size/alignment, lock-free evidence and any out-of-line support. Develop that evidence in [PR-T25-03](#pr-t25-03).

<a id="t25-08"></a>

### T25.08 — Memory-order reasoning

Relaxed ordering preserves atomicity but does not publish unrelated data. A release followed by an acquire that observes its publication can order those data accesses; seq_cst adds a specified order, not universal synchronization magic.

Worked publication: writer W initializes ordinary payload, then release-stores ready=1; reader R acquire-loads the value 1 from that store before reading payload. The read-from link supplies the synchronization edge and orders those payload actions. An acquire load that reads the initial zero does not supply that edge, and a later mutation still needs its own ownership/ordering protocol.

Investigate: Implement and diagram one single-owner publication handoff, then analyze a relaxed-only counterexample. A common mistake is: A larger observed counter automatically orders every associated payload write. Evidence: The diagram names the exact read-from and synchronizes-with edge; consume/fence questions remain edition-sensitive. Develop that evidence in [PR-T25-03](#pr-t25-03).

<a id="t25-09"></a>

### T25.09 — Compare-exchange

Compare-exchange updates expected on failure, and weak operations may fail spuriously. Failure order applies to the load side and cannot request release behavior. Ownership transfers only at the successful transition.

Investigate: Implement a bounded CAS state transition with a scripted spurious failure backend. A common mistake is: A failed CAS leaves expected unchanged or transfers the object anyway. Evidence: Retry traces show expected-value updates, valid order pairs and exactly one ownership transfer. Develop that evidence in [PR-T25-03](#pr-t25-03).

<a id="t25-10"></a>

### T25.10 — Progress and scheduling hazards

Deadlock forms a wait cycle; livelock changes state without useful progress; starvation denies a particular participant service. Scheduler priorities can also invert effective access to a resource.

Investigate: Construct one trace for each hazard and repair a two-lock order violation. A common mistake is: Short critical sections prove fairness or bounded response. Evidence: A wait-for graph and participant-level progress accounting distinguish the guarantees actually supplied. Develop that evidence in [PR-T25-04](#pr-t25-04).

Retain a separate evidence item for each objective below. Meeting one objective does not establish the others.

<a id="t25-11"></a>

### T25.11 — Cache and locality effects

Different variables can contend through one cache line even without a language-level race. Partitioning and batching can reduce traffic, but padding choices depend on the measured platform and object alignment.

Investigate: Compare adjacent versus separated per-thread counters after controlling useful work. A common mistake is: Cache-line separation changes the correctness memory model. Evidence: The measurement records layout, synchronization work and useful computation separately. Develop that evidence in [PR-T25-04](#pr-t25-04).

### T25.12 — Concurrency validation

Race detectors observe supported executions and instrumentation; stress explores schedules; deterministic scheduling makes a failure repeatable. None replaces an ordering and lifetime argument.

Investigate: Run the queue through forced schedules and a supported race detector, preserving minimized failures. A common mistake is: A clean sanitizer run is a proof for all schedules. Evidence: The evidence bundle combines explicit invariants, schedule traces and bounded tool claims. Develop that evidence in [PR-T25-05](#pr-t25-05).

## Reading guidance

The essential spine below is deliberately narrow. Assign only the exact inspected registry locators shown; no whole book, standard or implementation is implied. Historical rationale does not replace a current contract, and one implementation does not create a portable guarantee. Keep a short discrepancy log linking each source claim to the target/configuration where it applies.

- **The Linux Programming Interface: A Linux and UNIX System Programming Handbook (First edition)** — `R-SYS-TLPI-2010`, exactly **§30.2.3 Testing a Condition Variable’s Predicate, pp. 647–648** (1 h). Protect the queue predicate with the same mutex used for waits. Compare the source claim with your project assumptions. The registry classifies this as primary; its inspection limits remain part of the assignment.

- **POSIX.1-2024 pthread_cond_wait family specification (Issue 8, 2024 edition)** — `R-SYS-POSIX-COND-2024`, exactly **RATIONALE — Condition Wait Semantics** (1 h). Handle spurious wakeups, timeout and predicate rechecking under the formal wait contract. Compare the source claim with your project assumptions. The registry classifies this as oracle; its inspection limits remain part of the assignment.

- **POSIX.1-2024 Base Definitions: General Concepts (Issue 8, 2024 edition)** — `R-SYS-POSIX-MEMORY-2024`, exactly **§4.15.1.2 Memory Order and Consistency** (1 h). Draw the memory-order relations before reasoning about concrete loads/stores. Compare the source claim with your project assumptions. The registry classifies this as oracle; its inspection limits remain part of the assignment.

- **POSIX.1-2024 Base Definitions: General Concepts (Issue 8, 2024 edition)** — `R-SYS-POSIX-MEMORY-2024`, exactly **§4.15.2 Memory Synchronization** (1 h). Distinguish mutex/condition synchronization from unrelated ordinary accesses. Compare the source claim with your project assumptions. The registry classifies this as oracle; its inspection limits remain part of the assignment.

- **C thread creation and join clauses (N3096 working draft, April 1, 2023)** — `R-SYS-C-THREADS-N3096`, exactly **7.28.1 Introduction — paragraphs 1–2 and thrd_t/thrd_start_t definitions** (1 h). Check optional C thread support and the distinct thrd_t/thrd_start_t definitions; preserve the later-draft cross-check limit. Compare the source claim with your project assumptions. The registry classifies this as oracle; its inspection limits remain part of the assignment.

- **C thread creation and join clauses (N3096 working draft, April 1, 2023)** — `R-SYS-C-THREADS-N3096`, exactly **7.28.5.1 The thrd_create function — synopsis, description and returns** (1 h). Map integer start results and thrd_create success/failure without importing a POSIX pointer signature. Compare the source claim with your project assumptions. The registry classifies this as oracle; its inspection limits remain part of the assignment.

- **C thread creation and join clauses (N3096 working draft, April 1, 2023)** — `R-SYS-C-THREADS-N3096`, exactly **7.28.5.6 The thrd_join function — synopsis, description and returns** (1 h). Identify the one join owner and integer result lifetime from the C join clause. Compare the source claim with your project assumptions. The registry classifies this as oracle; its inspection limits remain part of the assignment.

- **POSIX thread creation and join (POSIX.1-2024 Issue 8)** — `R-SYS-POSIX-THREAD-LIFECYCLE-2024`, exactly **pthread_create — SYNOPSIS, DESCRIPTION, RETURN VALUE and ERRORS** (1 h). Map POSIX attributes, pointer-returning start and direct error-number status to the single implemented worker. Compare the source claim with your project assumptions. The registry classifies this as oracle; its inspection limits remain part of the assignment.

- **POSIX thread creation and join (POSIX.1-2024 Issue 8)** — `R-SYS-POSIX-THREAD-LIFECYCLE-2024`, exactly **pthread_join — SYNOPSIS, DESCRIPTION, RETURN VALUE and ERRORS** (1 h). Apply POSIX join ownership/result rules, including the explicit prohibition on C-created thread-result mixing. Compare the source claim with your project assumptions. The registry classifies this as oracle; its inspection limits remain part of the assignment.

See [guide-reading](#guide-reading) and [guide-standards](#guide-standards) for edition and evidence distinctions. Additional elective/API investigations require inspecting their precise version-specific passages before treating them as assigned authority.

## Mastery gate and feedback

Explain one positive path and one failure/counterexample for every subtopic without reading your implementation. Submit each project’s leaf-objective checklist with a distinct evidence item; shared runs may support several items only when the relation is explained. Re-run the saved independent fixture verifier, then reproduce at least one artifact from a clean environment. Passing those checks is evidence within their scope, not full-domain certification.

If an invariant, lifetime or environment claim cannot be defended, return to its project’s smallest trace and remediate the named entry knowledge. If a tool result disagrees with reasoning, minimize before changing expected results. A module passes when all core projects and awareness duties are accepted; elective implementation gaps remain visible. Use [guide-assessment](#guide-assessment) and [guide-audit](#guide-audit) for review records.

## Consolidation and transfer

After at least one day, reconstruct a selected contract and failing trace from memory, then apply one changed capacity/backend/target assumption. Explain which evidence survives and which must be regenerated. Transfer the dependency, ownership, representation or ordering ledger into the next project rather than copying an unexplained implementation. Record the delayed correction in the consolidation budget; see [guide-integrations](#guide-integrations) and [guide-workload](#guide-workload).

## Environment and limits

Use the declared Linux x86-64 environment for hosted observations and profile-specific adapters for portable components. Record compiler, linker, OS/library, architecture and configuration. Synthetic fixtures certify their declared static/reference calculations only. Unavailable target runs, unsupported instrumentation and hardware-dependent results are reported explicitly; emulator results do not prove STM32 electrical/peripheral behavior. No privileged host operation is required by a core project. See [guide-laboratory](#guide-laboratory), [guide-profiles](#guide-profiles) and [guide-inventory](#guide-inventory) before changing a boundary.

## Purpose and outcomes

Reach core awareness of concurrent histories, progress, identity, reclamation and kernel boundaries. Optional implementations have separate gates; awareness diagrams never certify a safe reclamation algorithm or loaded kernel module. The intended result is a mechanism you can explain, a bounded artifact you can inspect and an evidence trail someone else can reproduce. The published workload includes 24 h of explicitly elective project work; a core-only route subtracts those project hours, without removing core awareness.

## Entry check and remediation

Construct a release/acquire publication graph and distinguish atomicity from a compound invariant. Remediate T25 memory-order/CAS work and T14 ring invariants; awareness starts only when these are explicit. Use [guide-entry](#guide-entry) for diagnostic evidence and [guide-roadmap](#guide-roadmap) for route choices. Domain numbers are coverage IDs, not an instruction to study them numerically.

## Component progression

**Progress and reclamation as separate claims.** Construct finite histories for linearization, identity reuse and reclamation. Compare thread completion with system-wide progress and state the scheduler assumptions.

Before implementation, predict this discriminating case: **A correct compare-and-swap on a recycled address that no longer denotes the original object.** Carry its evidence into the projects below. Reuse one accepted component revision; new projects charge their new mechanism or experiment, not a second implementation of the old one.

Follow the [project route](#guide-project-route) for ordering. Domain numbers are reference categories. The [laboratory](#guide-laboratory) and [shared contract cards](#guide-component-contracts) separate automatic execution from reasoning, transfer and physical observations.

## Study sequence and teaching

Work through the mechanism notes in order within each project, alternating hand prediction with observation. Preserve the first counterexample rather than only a final green test. Full implementations belong to the projects; these notes explain what they must establish.


<a id="t26-01"></a>

### T26.01 — Concurrent-object specifications

A concurrent object is specified by permitted operation histories. Linearizability asks whether completed operations can be placed at single points consistent with real-time order; a valid memory execution alone does not supply that abstract history.

Investigate: Classify small queue histories and nominate a linearization point for each successful operation. A common mistake is: Memory-model consistency implies FIFO linearizability. Evidence: A sequential-history witness or contradiction is supplied for each declared fixture. Develop that evidence in [PR-T26-01](#pr-t26-01).


#### Evidence checklist

Retain a separate evidence item for each objective below. Meeting one objective does not establish the others.

<a id="t26-01-b"></a>


- **T26.01.b** Distinguish linearizability from memory-model consistency. **Disposition:** awareness. **Activity:** [PR-T26-01](#pr-t26-01).


<a id="t26-01-c"></a>


- **T26.01.c** Identify candidate linearization points in a concrete structure. **Disposition:** awareness. **Activity:** [PR-T26-01](#pr-t26-01).


<a id="t26-02"></a>

### T26.02 — Progress guarantees

Progress claims have different quantifiers: some participant makes progress, this participant completes, or an isolated participant completes. Allocation, atomics and scheduling can weaken the claim outside the core algorithm.

Investigate: Compare blocking/obstruction-free/lock-free/wait-free claims against declared stalled-participant traces. A common mistake is: Lock-free means every operation has a fixed completion bound. Evidence: The claim names participants, steps and external assumptions instead of reporting only aggregate throughput. Develop that evidence in [PR-T26-01](#pr-t26-01).

<a id="t26-03"></a>

### T26.03 — SPSC structures

An SPSC queue partitions responsibility: producer publishes occupied slots and consumer releases them for reuse. Counter wrap and slot lifetime require an explicit arithmetic model, not informal head/tail intuition.

Investigate: Analyze a bounded SPSC publication/reuse graph; optionally implement it after the core awareness gate. A common mistake is: Single producer/consumer removes all ordering requirements. Evidence: The slot state trace and wrap proof identify both publication and reclamation edges. Develop that evidence in [PR-T26-01](#pr-t26-01), [PR-T26-04](#pr-t26-04).


#### Evidence checklist

Retain a separate evidence item for each objective below. Meeting one objective does not establish the others.

<a id="t26-04"></a>

### T26.04 — MPSC and MPMC structures

Multiple producers add reservation states distinct from publication. A producer that reserves then stalls can affect consumers and other producers differently depending on the algorithm.

Investigate: Study the inspected Michael–Scott algorithm or a fully declared slot protocol and trace contention/cancellation. A common mistake is: Adding CAS to an SPSC head creates a complete MPMC design. Evidence: Every slot/node has a named owner and the trace separates reservation, publication and completion assumptions. Develop that evidence in [PR-T26-01](#pr-t26-01), [PR-T26-05](#pr-t26-05).

Retain a separate evidence item for each objective below. Meeting one objective does not establish the others.

<a id="t26-05"></a>

### T26.05 — ABA and identity

ABA occurs when a value changes away and back while its object identity or lifetime changes. A tag can distinguish reuse only until wrap or unavailable atomic width defeats its assumptions.

Investigate: Construct a stale compare-exchange with object reuse and analyze generation/tag alternatives. A common mistake is: Equal pointer bits prove the same live object remained there. Evidence: The trace explicitly names object identities, reuse and tag-wrap limits. Develop that evidence in [PR-T26-02](#pr-t26-02), [PR-T26-05](#pr-t26-05).


#### Evidence checklist

<a id="t26-06"></a>

### T26.06 — Hazard pointers

Hazard protection announces a candidate pointer, then validates that the source still names the same live object before dereferencing. Retirement differs from reclamation; a scan must establish the scheme’s protection obligations.

Investigate: Perform an awareness-level protection/validation/retire timeline and account for stalled/departing participants. A common mistake is: Publishing a pointer once is enough to make arbitrary reclamation safe. Evidence: The timeline identifies each protected interval and retained node; implementation requires an independently inspected complete protocol. Develop that evidence in [PR-T26-02](#pr-t26-02), [PR-T26-05](#pr-t26-05).

<a id="t26-07"></a>

### T26.07 — Epoch and quiescence schemes

Epoch schemes delay reuse until participants that could hold old references pass a required quiescent boundary. A stalled active participant can retain old objects indefinitely unless failure policy changes the assumptions.

Investigate: Model retirement epochs and participant progress with an explicit active/inactive table. A common mistake is: Elapsed wall-clock time alone completes a grace period. Evidence: A reclamation eligibility table and retained-memory calculation include a stalled participant. Develop that evidence in [PR-T26-02](#pr-t26-02), [PR-T26-05](#pr-t26-05).

<a id="t26-08"></a>

### T26.08 — RCU concepts

RCU separates publishing a new version, readers using a version and reclaiming an old version after the appropriate grace period. Userspace libraries and the Linux kernel expose different contexts and APIs.

Investigate: Analyze a read/copy/publish/grace/reclaim sequence and classify model-specific obligations. A common mistake is: Completing a publication store immediately permits freeing the old object. Evidence: An object-lifetime diagram names the grace-period owner and refuses to infer one environment’s API rules from another. Develop that evidence in [PR-T26-02](#pr-t26-02), [PR-T26-05](#pr-t26-05).


#### Evidence checklist

Retain a separate evidence item for each objective below. Meeting one objective does not establish the others.

<a id="t26-09"></a>

### T26.09 — Kernel programming boundaries

Kernel code runs under version-specific build and execution contracts. User pointers need checked access mechanisms, allocation flags encode context constraints, and some contexts cannot sleep.

Investigate: Create an awareness dossier for an isolated version-matched kernel test environment and classify candidate calls by context. A common mistake is: A userspace pointer or allocator contract can be reused directly in a kernel callback. Evidence: The dossier names isolation, API/version sources and prohibited operations before any optional implementation. Develop that evidence in [PR-T26-03](#pr-t26-03).


#### Evidence checklist

Retain a separate evidence item for each objective below. Meeting one objective does not establish the others.

<a id="t26-09-b"></a>

<a id="t26-10"></a>

### T26.10 — Kernel memory and lifetime models

The kernel memory model uses its own marked accesses and ordering primitives. Module removal must also wait for callbacks/work that retain code or objects; ordering alone does not extend lifetime.

Worked kernel lifetime graph: external producer -> module_text; queued/running work -> module_text and device_object. With one queued and one running instance in the declared model, smp_mb preserves all these lifetime edges. An unload attempt therefore fails the model gate. Stop and wait for every producer first, then let cancel_work_sync return under its no-racing-enqueue and permitted-context preconditions. Only then are pending/running work zero; release the object and consider code removal eligible within this narrow graph. That eligibility is not a real-module verdict: any IRQ, timer, RCU, delayed work or other registration adds a distinct obligation outside this fixture.

Investigate: Contrast a portable C ordering graph with the inspected LKMM relations and model callback unload states. A common mistake is: A memory barrier proves a callback cannot run after unloading its code. Evidence: Separate ordering and lifetime ledgers identify the drain/grace obligations; kernel experiments remain optional and isolated. Develop that evidence in [PR-T26-03](#pr-t26-03).


#### Evidence checklist

Retain a separate evidence item for each objective below. Meeting one objective does not establish the others.

<a id="t26-10-b"></a>


- **T26.10.b** Analyze module unloading, callback lifetime, and deferred work. **Disposition:** awareness. **Activity:** [PR-T26-03](#pr-t26-03).

## Reading guidance

The essential spine below is deliberately narrow. Assign only the exact inspected registry locators shown; no whole book, standard or implementation is implied. Historical rationale does not replace a current contract, and one implementation does not create a portable guarantee. Keep a short discrepancy log linking each source claim to the target/configuration where it applies.

- **Simple, Fast, and Practical Non-Blocking and Blocking Concurrent Queue Algorithms (PODC 1996 paper)** — `R-SYS-MICHAEL-SCOTT-1996`, exactly **§3.1 Safety** (1 h). Identify historical queue safety assumptions before proposing modern atomic spellings. Compare the source claim with your project assumptions. The registry classifies this as supplement; its inspection limits remain part of the assignment.

- **Explanation of the Linux-Kernel Memory Consistency Model (Linux v6.12 tag)** — `R-SYS-LKMM-6-12`, exactly **THE PROGRAM ORDER RELATION: po AND po-loc** (1 h). Read program-order relations in LKMM without treating them as ISO C user-space contracts. Compare the source claim with your project assumptions. The registry classifies this as source; its inspection limits remain part of the assignment.

- **Linux kernel memory barriers (Linux v6.12 documentation)** — `R-SYS-LINUX-BARRIERS-6-12`, exactly **SMP BARRIER PAIRING** (1 h). Draw paired kernel ordering operations and preserve the barrier guide’s hardware/compiler limitations. Compare the source claim with your project assumptions. The registry classifies this as supplement; its inspection limits remain part of the assignment.

- **Linux workqueue cancellation and drain APIs (Linux 6.12 documentation)** — `R-SYS-LINUX-WORK-CANCEL-6-12`, exactly **Workqueue — cancel_work_sync: parameters, description and return** (1 h). Explain the no-racing-enqueue and calling-context preconditions for synchronous work drain; distinguish cancellation from mere ordering. Compare the source claim with your project assumptions. The registry classifies this as oracle; its inspection limits remain part of the assignment.

See [guide-reading](#guide-reading) and [guide-standards](#guide-standards) for edition and evidence distinctions. Additional elective/API investigations require inspecting their precise version-specific passages before treating them as assigned authority.

## Mastery gate and feedback

Explain one positive path and one failure/counterexample for every subtopic without reading your implementation. Submit each project’s leaf-objective checklist with a distinct evidence item; shared runs may support several items only when the relation is explained. Re-run the saved independent fixture verifier, then reproduce at least one artifact from a clean environment. Passing those checks is evidence within their scope, not full-domain certification.

If an invariant, lifetime or environment claim cannot be defended, return to its project’s smallest trace and remediate the named entry knowledge. If a tool result disagrees with reasoning, minimize before changing expected results. A module passes when all core projects and awareness duties are accepted; elective implementation gaps remain visible. Use [guide-assessment](#guide-assessment) and [guide-audit](#guide-audit) for review records.

## Consolidation and transfer

After at least one day, reconstruct a selected contract and failing trace from memory, then apply one changed capacity/backend/target assumption. Explain which evidence survives and which must be regenerated. Transfer the dependency, ownership, representation or ordering ledger into the next project rather than copying an unexplained implementation. Record the delayed correction in the consolidation budget; see [guide-integrations](#guide-integrations) and [guide-workload](#guide-workload).

## Environment and limits

Use the declared Linux x86-64 environment for hosted observations and profile-specific adapters for portable components. Record compiler, linker, OS/library, architecture and configuration. Synthetic fixtures certify their declared static/reference calculations only. Unavailable target runs, unsupported instrumentation and hardware-dependent results are reported explicitly; emulator results do not prove STM32 electrical/peripheral behavior. No privileged host operation is required by a core project. See [guide-laboratory](#guide-laboratory), [guide-profiles](#guide-profiles) and [guide-inventory](#guide-inventory) before changing a boundary.

## Purpose and outcomes

Establish ownership of a bare-metal image from reset through entry. Every copied byte, stack assumption and runtime dependency should be observable in the image and in a bounded startup trace.

## Entry check and remediation

Trace load/run addresses, identify a linker symbol versus a C object, and explain why calling C needs an ABI-valid stack. If any answer is weak, repair the corresponding T08/T09/T11 leaf before flashing. Draw the selected board/core/device documentation boundary and check the fixture's hexadecimal regions by hand.

Use [guide-entry](#guide-entry) for the diagnostic policy and [guide-roadmap](#guide-roadmap) for route order. Only the stated prelude leaves must precede a dependent project.

## Component progression

**Reset-to-main as an inspected memory transform.** Name reset state, vector ownership, stack region and load/run addresses. Verify copy, zero and retained ranges before trusting global values.

Before implementation, predict this discriminating case: **A valid link map paired with an incorrect startup zero range.** Carry its evidence into the projects below. Reuse one accepted component revision; new projects charge their new mechanism or experiment, not a second implementation of the old one.

Follow the [project route](#guide-project-route) for ordering. Domain numbers are reference categories. The [laboratory](#guide-laboratory) and [shared contract cards](#guide-component-contracts) separate automatic execution from reasoning, transfer and physical observations.

## Study sequence and teaching


<a id="t27-01"></a>

### T27.01 — Hardware evidence and target selection

The MCU, package, board revision and emulator are four identities. An F439ZI board record must distinguish RM0090, DS9484, UM1974, ES0206 and the Arm core guide. Build an evidence ledger with memory banks and observed boot configuration, then compare it to the synthetic target fixture. Assuming every Cortex-M4 board has STM32 registers is the central trap. Your evidence must mark each claim as document-derived, image-derived, emulator-observed or physical-board-observed.

Apply this mechanism in [PR-T27-01](#pr-t27-01).

<a id="t27-02"></a>

### T27.02 — Reset and boot ownership

Reset begins under hardware/ROM ownership before application startup. Boot selection changes the aliased vector source; a debugger may establish state a cold power cycle never supplies. Draw the Flash/system-memory/SRAM decision and annotate who owns clocks, interrupts and reset-cause capture at handoff. Treat watchdog, software and power resets as separate trials. Evidence is an observed PC/vector-source trace plus a reset-state ledger; 'it runs after loading in the debugger' does not establish standalone boot.

Apply this mechanism in [PR-T27-01](#pr-t27-01).

<a id="t27-03"></a>

### T27.03 — Vector table

The first vector word supplies the initial stack and subsequent words select exception handlers under the architecture's encoding rules. Retaining the section in the linked image matters as much as defining the array. Construct a vector section, inspect its bytes/symbols and reject a reset address outside executable Flash. A linker symbol's presence does not prove placement. For bootloader offsets, state alignment/VTOR rules from the chosen implementation and preserve a before/after relocation inspection.

Apply this mechanism in [PR-T27-02](#pr-t27-02).

<a id="t27-04"></a>

### T27.04 — Stack initialization

The stack descends within a reserved region and must satisfy AAPCS alignment before compiled C is called. A public call boundary requires eight-byte alignment even if ordinary stack operations preserve four. Budget call depth plus nested exception frames and any FPU extension; a canary reports tested usage, not all possible paths. Select an initial stack from the fixture, demonstrate alignment checks, and explain how overflow enters a bounded failure path rather than assuming unused RAM is safe.

Apply this mechanism in [PR-T27-02](#pr-t27-02).


#### Evidence checklist

Retain a separate evidence item for each objective below. Meeting one objective does not establish the others.


<a id="t27-04-a"></a>

<a id="t27-05"></a>

### T27.05 — Initialized and zeroed data

An initialized object has load bytes in Flash and execution storage in RAM; zero-initialized objects need clearing, while explicitly retained regions need a different policy. Implement startup copying/clearing from linker ranges, including a second RAM bank, and use distinct sentinels to expose overlap. Clearing 'all RAM' destroys retained evidence. Compare the exact expected memory transformation with debugger reads before main and prove each loop's bounds without relying on libc being initialized.

Apply this mechanism in [PR-T27-03](#pr-t27-03).

Early setup must establish only the prerequisites actually used by startup and the application. Configure the F439 clock path with readiness checks and bounded failure, respecting disabled-PLL configuration and applicable peripheral-clock errata. Do not call floating-point code before selecting and documenting the core/FPU ABI/state policy. Test a never-ready clock in the logical adapter. Evidence includes the ordered access trace and an actual target clock observation when a frequency claim is made.

Apply this mechanism in [PR-T27-04](#pr-t27-04).

### T27.07 — Runtime hooks and entry

A reset handler is a runtime policy: it decides whether initialization arrays run, which hooks exist and what happens if application entry returns. Calling main does not automatically provide libc, allocation or constructors. Implement a named entry contract with a deterministic halt/recovery return policy and one supported initialization-hook sequence. Evidence is a symbol/dependency audit and an ordered hook trace, including an unsupported-hook rejection rather than a silent skipped initializer.

Apply this mechanism in [PR-T27-03](#pr-t27-03).

First annotate a vendor startup file against its linker symbols and core assumptions, then replace selected copying/vector/entry pieces with your own minimal implementation. Your independent implementation must reach the same sentinel state from an actual reset while preserving documented differences.

<a id="t27-09"></a>

### T27.09 — Retained state and boot handoff

Retained bytes need a validity protocol because reset does not imply they describe the current image. Use a magic, version, length and checksum for accidental corruption, then reject invalid or incompatible records before consuming payload. A boot handoff also owns vector base, stack, pending interrupts and clocks. Test stale versions and interrupted record writes in the fixture. Checksums establish consistency under this model, not cryptographic authenticity or freshness against an attacker.

Apply this mechanism in [PR-T27-05](#pr-t27-05).

### T27.10 — Bring-up verification

Bring-up observations should get simpler as startup gets earlier: debugger memory, one register marker, then minimal GPIO/UART output after prerequisites exist. Deliberately break one vector, one copy range and one clock-ready condition; classify the failure before editing code. Repeat without debugger initialization and power-cycle the physical board. An emulator trace can establish its own machine behavior, but cannot establish Nucleo pin levels or cold-start electrical behavior.

Apply this mechanism in [PR-T27-05](#pr-t27-05).

## Reading guidance

Read the bounded selections before the corresponding project, then annotate one contract or assumption you will test. The assigned reading table is generated from the exact inspected locators. Spend the remaining reading budget on original teaching, worked traces and target documentation comparisons, not whole uninspected chapters.

**STM32F405/415, STM32F407/417, STM32F427/437 and STM32F429/439 advanced Arm-based 32-bit MCUs — 2.4 Boot configuration (1 h):** Trace reset vector source.

**Procedure Call Standard for the Arm Architecture — 6.2.1.2 Stack constraints at a public interface (1 h):** Establish the C call boundary.

**CMSIS-Core (Cortex-M): Startup File startup_<device>.c — Startup File startup_<device>.c (1 h):** Compare generic startup structure.

**STM32 Nucleo-144 boards (MB1137) — Introduction (1 h):** Identify board applicability.

**Shared scope limit — STM32F405/415, STM32F407/417, STM32F427/437 and STM32F429/439 advanced Arm-based 32-bit MCUs:** Inspected Rev 21; newer Rev 22 delta uninspected. F439 RCC is chapter 6, not earlier-family chapter 7. Additional authoring inspection supports bounded 7-bit I2C transmit/single-byte receive and full-duplex SPI sequencing; optimized I2C multibyte/NACK timing and full error chapters remain outside scope. ADC sampling/trigger/single conversion are inspected, but analog electrical accuracy and Stop/Standby recipes are not. Physical timings, package pins and device electrical conditions need DS/board evidence and measurement.

**Shared scope limit — Procedure Call Standard for the Arm Architecture:** Select the actual ABI variant and floating-point options used by the toolchain; this document does not choose a board memory map or linker layout.

**Shared scope limit — CMSIS-Core (Cortex-M): Startup File startup_<device>.c:** Generic template contains adaptation TODOs and Armv8-M stack-limit/sealing operations; it must not be copied verbatim to Cortex-M4. Device startup and linker/runtime initialization must be inspected for the selected compiler.

**Shared scope limit — STM32 Nucleo-144 boards (MB1137):** Inspected Rev 8, not current Rev 11. Board revision, actual solder bridges and clock population must be recorded on physical hardware; described defaults are not a measurement of the learner's board.

See [guide-reading](#guide-reading) for access/provenance and [guide-standards](#guide-standards) for the language baseline.

## Implementation projects

- [PR-T27-01 — Target and reset evidence ledger](#pr-t27-01), 4 h, core, profile E. Build a target/reset ledger for the exact MCU, package, board and emulator.

- [PR-T27-02 — Vector and stack image](#pr-t27-02), 6 h, core, profile E. Create a retained vector section and linker-reserved stack satisfying the basic selected ABI.

- [PR-T27-03 — Startup memory and runtime hooks](#pr-t27-03), 8 h, core, profile E. Implement initialized-data copying and zeroing from explicit linker ranges, preserve declared retained bytes, and support a documented hook/entry/return policy without hidden hosted CRT services.

- [PR-T27-04 — Minimal startup replacement](#pr-t27-04), 8 h, core, profile E. Annotate vendor startup, then replace vector/copy/entry pieces with an independent minimal image and a bounded early-clock setup.

- [PR-T27-05 — Retained state and standalone boot](#pr-t27-05), 6 h, core, profile E. Implement retained-record validity and documented boot handoff responsibilities, then verify standalone reset operation with bounded early diagnostics.

Project hours are the implementation plus verification budget, counted once. The optional-project-hour metadata identifies extensions included in this complete-module ledger; consult [guide-workload](#guide-workload) when selecting a core-only route.

## Mastery gate and feedback

Start the minimal image from reset, identify vector/stack/copy/hook evidence and explain a deliberately broken range. Physical-board completion includes standalone power-cycle success; emulator completion is a separately labeled stage. Failure in early entry requires shrinking to a marker before adding drivers.

For every linked objective, retain a separately labeled explanation, implementation/analysis artifact and check. Use [guide-assessment](#guide-assessment) for the rubric; one passing fixture does not establish all three objectives of a topic.

## Consolidation and transfer

A week later, relocate a small data section to another verified RAM bank and change the retained-record version. Predict the map and startup changes, then demonstrate rejection of old state. Review how a bootloader would change reset ownership.

Use [T37](#t37) to deepen ISA, clocked-state, bus, memory and exception reasoning. Carry the actual startup/linker/map evidence into [T38](#t38)–[T41](#t41); a host model cannot replace board reachability or physical observations.

## Environment and limits

Use [guide-profiles](#guide-profiles) to declare the dependency boundary, [guide-laboratory](#guide-laboratory) for installed tools and hardware, and [guide-audit](#guide-audit) for image/call-graph evidence. Fixtures are original deterministic mathematical or synthetic-protocol data. Run `python tools/verify_embedded_fixtures.py` from the curriculum root to recompute their expectations. This oracle checks fixtures, not learner code.

Host adapters establish only their declared state-machine semantics. QEMU mps2-an386 establishes its Arm FPGA machine behavior; it does not implement STM32F439 registers. Physical-board completion requires the exact board/revision/pin/clock evidence. RM0090 Rev 21 and UM1974 Rev 8 are the inspected revisions; newer portal revisions require delta review before adopting changed procedures. No simulated timing or analog result is a physical measurement.

Use [guide-inventory](#guide-inventory) to find supplied data and [guide-integrations](#guide-integrations) for later cross-module work.

# T28 — MMIO, peripherals, and driver construction

| Track | Status | Hours | Dependency profiles |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| bare-metal | core | 75 | C, E |

**Prerequisites:** [T04](#t04), [T18](#t18), [T20](#t20), [T27](#t27).

| Reading | Implementation | Verification | Assessment | Consolidation |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 12 | 33 | 17 | 8 | 5 |

## Purpose and outcomes

Turn documented peripheral transactions into bounded driver state machines and portable service contracts. Begin with side-effect models, then replace only the adapter with verified target accesses.

## Entry check and remediation

Derive a bit mask, distinguish volatile from publication, trace a callback failure, and calculate a divisor from a stated clock. Repair T04 bit/arithmetic or T18 contract/test skills selectively. Pin the exact board/package/pins and clock tree before connecting external buses.

Use [guide-entry](#guide-entry) for the diagnostic policy and [guide-roadmap](#guide-roadmap) for route order. Only the stated prelude leaves must precede a dependent project.

## Component progression

**A bounded peripheral transaction.** Read the device's register semantics before designing the driver state machine. Separate controller protocol, electrical interface, clock source and completion condition.

Before implementation, predict this discriminating case: **A read-modify-write accidentally clearing a write-one-to-clear status bit.** Carry its evidence into the projects below. Reuse one accepted component revision; new projects charge their new mechanism or experiment, not a second implementation of the old one.

Follow the [project route](#guide-project-route) for ordering. Domain numbers are reference categories. The [laboratory](#guide-laboratory) and [shared contract cards](#guide-component-contracts) separate automatic execution from reasoning, transfer and physical observations.

## Study sequence and teaching


<a id="t28-01"></a>

### T28.01 — Register documentation

Registers are transactions, not just integers in a struct. Record access width, offset, reserved-bit policy, reset value and side effects for each selected register. In the synthetic adapter, reading DATA consumes a byte and writing one to STATUS acknowledges selected flags; reproduce these effects in a logged model. The trap is using a generic read-modify-write on a side-effect register. Evidence includes a minimal legal access sequence and a rejected illegal width/reserved-bit write.

Apply this mechanism in [PR-T28-01](#pr-t28-01).


#### Evidence checklist

Retain a separate evidence item for each objective below. Meeting one objective does not establish the others.

<a id="t28-02"></a>

### T28.02 — MMIO access rules

Volatile makes selected accesses observable to the compiler under the implementation contract; it does not make a multi-access update atomic or publish ordinary shared data. GPIO BSRR provides a dedicated atomic bit operation, whereas reading ODR and writing a modified value leaves an interrupt window. Implement both against a scripted interleaving and demonstrate the lost update. Evidence is the access log plus the correct BSRR mask; do not claim a host RAM variable models all MMIO behavior.

Apply this mechanism in [PR-T28-01](#pr-t28-01).

Retain a separate evidence item for each objective below. Meeting one objective does not establish the others.

### T28.03 — Clock and reset control

A peripheral's baud/timer settings are meaningful only with its actual input clock. Enable/reset the selected peripheral, respect the relevant post-enable delay, and check readiness with a bounded timeout. The F439 RCC chapter is chapter 6. Derive each bus/timer input from a recorded clock tree, then invalidate configuration on a clock change. The misconception is that SystemCoreClock automatically equals every peripheral clock. Retain the calculation and scope or logic-analyzer measurement.

Apply this mechanism in [PR-T28-02](#pr-t28-02).

GPIO mode, output type, pull and alternate function solve different electrical/routing problems. Write a configuration table before touching pins, then use BSRR for output set/reset and a stable-sample debounce state machine for input. A pull-up does not replace a documented external bus resistor requirement. Test bouncing samples and atomic updates in the fixture; on hardware inspect package pin/board routing and measure levels without driving an unknown external circuit.

Apply this mechanism in [PR-T28-01](#pr-t28-01).

<a id="t28-05"></a>

### T28.05 — UART

The initial UART contract is bounded 8N1 polling, then an interrupt/DMA adapter can preserve the same service interface. For OVER8=0, BRR encodes the rounded peripheral-clock/baud divisor; report the resulting baud error. TXE permits another data-register write, while TC means the frame has finished. Receive by reading data only when RXNE is set; capture ORE/FE/NF status and the documented clearing order. Evidence includes bytes, timeout/overflow outcomes and a physical waveform for any baud claim.

Apply this mechanism in [PR-T28-02](#pr-t28-02).

<a id="t28-06"></a>

### T28.06 — Timers and PWM

For an up-counting timer with known timer clock, frequency is f_timer/((PSC+1)*(ARR+1)); compare values define duty relative to ARR+1. Preloads separate the written value from the active value until an update event. Implement a configuration calculator and update protocol, test zero/full duty and rollover, then measure actual output. A register value that represents the desired frequency does not prove it occurs on the pin. Timestamp precision also includes capture/clock uncertainty.

Apply this mechanism in [PR-T28-03](#pr-t28-03).

<a id="t28-07"></a>

### T28.07 — SPI

SPI clocks both directions even when the application only wants to send. The contract specifies CPOL/CPHA, eight-bit words, MSB-first order, GPIO chip select and paired transmit/receive ownership. Wait for TXE before each write, consume RXNE, and finish the selected full-duplex transfer by waiting for TXE then BSY clear before release. A device command protocol is separate from controller sequencing. Test partial progress and timeout with deterministic byte pairs; validate actual clock/CS timing on a verified connection.

Apply this mechanism in [PR-T28-04](#pr-t28-04).
